# Machine-readability reference fixtures

Synthetic input and selected outcomes from Harunobu 0.2.2 at commit
`88014ff9cfe685d4e0e5f24a2d4d2e021ca3fd9f`, standard mode, AI disabled.
Source: https://github.com/digital-go-jp/machine_readability_rule

`structure.xlsx` contains a data merge, hidden row and column, and a formula.
`header-merge.xlsx` contains a header merge, which Harunobu reports as
information while passing L1-12. `data.csv` is a simple CSV; Excel-only rules
are absent from that reference result. The JSON records only L1-12, L1-13 and
L2-06; it is not a complete Harunobu report or a conformance result.

Regenerate using a clean checkout of the pinned commit and `uv sync --frozen`,
then run `python3 scripts/machine-readability-reference.py /path/to/harunobu`.
The Rust scanner detects structural candidates on the live sheet. It does not
infer tables or headers, so its findings are not Harunobu pass/fail results.

The Harunobu sample implementation is distributed under MIT; its rule data
and documentation use PDL 1.0. This fixture and recorded result were generated
for ibisOffice and are not an official Digital Agency certification.
See https://github.com/digital-go-jp/machine_readability_rule#ライセンスについて

`harunobu-character-reference.json` records `_detect_in_cell` results from
the same pinned Harunobu version for synthetic Unicode examples. The live
scanner checks the whole sheet and does not apply table, encoding, or score
semantics; these examples do not establish full rule parity.

`harunobu-scoring-reference.json` records the default `LevelScorer` results
for synthetic rule outcomes at all three levels, including skipped and fatal
rules, default severity, saturation, and repeated rule IDs. It is generated
by `scripts/machine-readability-reference.py`. This tests scoring only, not
rule execution, table detection, or end-to-end parity.

`harunobu-workbook-rules-reference.json` records synthetic L1-01 and L1-02
outcomes with supplied file format and table regions. It does not test file
signature validation or layout detection.

`harunobu-csv-diagnostics-reference.json` records raw diagnostics for
synthetic CSV and TSV, including quoting, embedded line breaks, field counts,
the bounded-sample and truncation limits, and 100 seeded synthetic inputs.
It does not test decoding bytes
or infer tables.

`harunobu-csv-rules-reference.json` records L1-14 and L1-15 rule outcomes
on those same diagnostics with a supplied table range.

`harunobu-character-rule-reference.json` records L1-08 outcomes for the same
text values under XLSX, UTF-8, and CP932 encoding policies, including Roman
classification codes and mixed warning/information cases.

`harunobu-csv-reader-reference.json` records synthetic CSV/TSV records and
reader errors, generated by `scripts/machine-readability-csv-reader-reference.py`
against the pinned Harunobu checkout. Empty fields, blank lines, malformed
quotes, carriage returns and embedded newlines are included. It validates the
byte-stream reader's decoded-text behavior, not the file-path reader.

`cp932-python-pairs.bin` contains Python CP932 decoding expectations for every
one- and two-byte sequence, generated by
`scripts/machine-readability-cp932-reference.py`. Each eight-byte little-endian
record contains two Unicode scalars; `0x110000` means no second scalar and
`0x110001` means an invalid sequence. It validates strict decoding, not every
possible longer sequence or ambiguous UTF-8 detection.

`harunobu-csv-layout-reference.json` connects four synthetic UTF-8, UTF-8 BOM,
and CP932 CSV/TSV inputs to detected table ranges and header rows. These cases
exercise a native byte-reader-to-layout path, not the UI, scoring, reports, or
all of Harunobu's detection and rule behavior.

`harunobu-xlsx-layout-reference.json` compares two synthetic XLSX files with
Harunobu's cell values, merge markers, and detected layout. The reader window is
provided explicitly; the adapter rejects non-General numeric formats until it
can determine date typing from authoritative source metadata.

`xlsx-cache-*.xlsx` and `harunobu-xlsx-formula-reference.json` are generated by
`scripts/machine-readability-xlsx-formula-reference.py`. They cover missing,
numeric, Boolean, string, formula-like string, and error formula caches. The
native adapter reads those caches from original XML because the editor model
may recalculate formulas when opening the file. These examples do not establish
complete XLSX compatibility or full Harunobu analysis.
